summary.text: An event is a subset of the sample space, and when the sample space is finite every subset is typically treated as an event.
For infinite sample spaces such as the real numbers, giving a probability to every subset runs into difficulties with badly behaved, nonmeasurable sets, so events are restricted to a smaller family.
In the measure-theoretic view an event is an element of a chosen σ-algebra, and a subset outside it is not an event and has no probability.

items.prompt: A die has six faces, so the sample space has a finite number of results. Could the group made of the faces one and five be treated as an event?

options.label: No, events must have at least three results
Yes, any subset of a finite sample space can be an event
No, only the whole list of results can be an event
Yes, but only if both faces are equally likely

items.explain: When the sample space is finite, any subset of it is typically an event.

items.prompt: Tomorrow's weather is described by the event 'it rains'. What else does that event automatically define?

options.label: A matching event for it not raining, giving a yes-or-no question
A second rainy day that must follow the first
A probability of one half for each result
A rule that no other event can be defined

items.explain: An event defines a complementary event, the event not occurring, and together they make a Bernoulli trial: did the event occur or not?

items.prompt: A measurement can be any real number. Why not simply declare every subset of the real numbers to be an event?

options.label: Because real numbers cannot be measured at all
Because there are too few subsets to choose from
Because finite sample spaces already use up all the subsets
Because badly behaved nonmeasurable sets resist getting probabilities

items.explain: Attempts to define probabilities for all subsets of the real numbers run into difficulties with nonmeasurable sets, so attention is restricted to a more limited family.

items.prompt: A subset of the sample space is left out of the chosen σ-algebra. Does that subset have a probability?

options.label: Yes, a very small one
Yes, equal to its complement's
Yes, but only when the sample space is finite
No, it is not an event

items.explain: Any subset that is not an element of the σ-algebra is not an event and does not have a probability.

items.prompt: A family of sets is called closed under complementation and countable unions. If one set is in the family, what else must be?

options.label: The set made of its complement
Every other set in the sample space
Only the empty set
Nothing, because one set is enough

items.explain: Being closed under complementation means the complement of any member is also a member, and a σ-algebra has this property.

items.prompt: A statistician has set up a sensible probability space. Will an event she cares about be missing from its σ-algebra?

options.label: Yes, since most useful events are left out
No, with a reasonable setup all events of interest are included
Yes, since only complements are included
No, since every subset is an event anyway

items.explain: With a reasonable specification of the probability space, all events of interest are elements of the σ-algebra.

paragraphs.heading: What an event is
paragraphs.text: In probability theory, an event is a set of outcomes of an experiment, that is, a piece of the sample space that is given a probability. One outcome can belong to many different events. Events in the same experiment are usually not equally likely, since they can hold very different groups of outcomes.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of events
paragraphs.text: An event made of just one outcome is called an elementary event, or atomic event; in set terms it is a singleton. An event with more than one possible outcome is a compound event. Every event also has a complementary event, the event not happening. Together the pair make a Bernoulli trial: did the event happen or not?

paragraphs.heading: When an event occurs
paragraphs.text: An event S occurs when the outcome x of the experiment lies inside S, written x ∈ S. So the probability that S occurs is simply the probability that the outcome lands in S. That probability is measured with respect to some probability measure.

paragraphs.heading: Finite versus infinite
paragraphs.text: When the sample space is finite, usually every subset counts as an event. That approach stops working well when the sample space is infinite, and especially when it is uncountably infinite. For many standard distributions, the normal distribution among them, the outcomes are the real numbers or part of them. Trying to give a probability to every subset of the real numbers runs into trouble with badly behaved, nonmeasurable sets. So attention has to be limited to a smaller family of subsets, and some subsets are left out of the events.

paragraphs.heading: The σ-algebra
paragraphs.text: The family used is a σ-algebra: a collection of subsets closed under taking complements and countable unions of its members. It is needed for standard tools such as joint and conditional probabilities to work. The most natural choice is the Borel sets, built from unions and intersections of intervals, though the larger class of Lebesgue measurable sets is more useful in practice. In this measure-theoretic picture an event is an element of the chosen σ-algebra, and a subset outside it is not an event and has no probability.

paragraphs.heading: In practice
paragraphs.text: With a sensible setup, every event of interest belongs to the σ-algebra anyway. And although events are formally subsets of a sample space Ω, they are often written as conditions on random variables. The set u < X ≤ v is one example.
